sentences.text: Being left out may feel, to your brain, a lot like physical pain.
So that sting when the group goes quiet is not you being dramatic.
In one study, people left out of a game showed brain activity that rose with their distress.
Another region was active too, and linked to less distress.
Feeling it doesn't mean something is wrong, it means people matter to you.

sources.title: Does rejection hurt? An fMRI study of social exclusion
sources.licence: abstract only, facts only, no text or figure reused

claims.claim: Participants were scanned while playing a virtual ball-tossing game in which they were ultimately excluded.
claims.excerpt: Participants were scanned while playing a virtual ball-tossing game in which they were ultimately excluded.
claims.context: Study design. The exclusion was inside a virtual game, not a real relationship or a message.

claims.claim: The study tested whether the brain bases of social pain are similar to those of physical pain, and its results paralleled results from physical pain studies.
claims.excerpt: tested the hypothesis that the brain bases of social pain are similar to those of physical pain. ... Paralleling results from physical pain studies
claims.context: One 2003 study. 'Paralleling' is the abstract's word; it does not say social and physical pain are the same.

claims.claim: The anterior cingulate cortex was more active during exclusion than inclusion and correlated positively with self-reported distress.
claims.excerpt: the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) was more active during exclusion than during inclusion and correlated positively with self-reported distress.
claims.context: A correlation between activity and reported distress, not proof that activity causes distress.

claims.claim: Right ventral prefrontal cortex was active during exclusion and correlated negatively with self-reported distress.
claims.excerpt: Right ventral prefrontal cortex (RVPFC) was active during exclusion and correlated negatively with self-reported distress.
claims.context: The authors suggest this region may regulate distress; that is their interpretation and is not stated as fact here.

claims.claim: The study measured brain activity that accompanied the reported distress of being excluded.
claims.excerpt: A neuroimaging study examined the neural correlates of social exclusion
claims.context: Frames the finding as accompanying activity ('neural correlates'), not a cause.
